# Size class sweep

Waste of the geometric table as a function of the growth factor, for the v1.0
configuration. Derivation and interpretation: [cost-model.md](cost-model.md).

| parameter | value |
|---|---|
| `s_min` (`min_class_bytes`) | 256 B |
| `s_max` (`max_class_bytes`) | 2097152 B (2 MiB) |
| `chunk_min` (`chunk_bytes`) | 2097152 B (2 MiB) |
| growth range | 1.10 to 2.00, step 0.01 |
| internal waste | closed form for log-uniform requests, normalised by assigned capacity |
| tail waste | mean of `tail_i / chunk_i` over classes, one unit of resident weight each |

Class counts come from the **rounded** table (`c_{i+1} = round_up(ceil(c_i·g), 256)`),
not from the closed form: the alignment rounding merges geometric steps, so `k` at
`g = 1.10` is 77 and not the 96 of `ceil(log_g R) + 1`.

## Minimum of `E[W_int] + E[W_tail]`

| growth | classes | internal waste | tail waste | total |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.10 | 77 | 4.618% | 5.558% | 10.176% |

The minimum sits on the lower edge of the swept range: with resident weight spread
evenly over the table, `E[W_int]` grows monotonically with `g` while `E[W_tail]` only
oscillates (see Table A), so the sum has no interior optimum. The objective above
therefore cannot pick 1.5 by itself — the justification for `g = 1.5` includes a term
this sweep does not model: a class retains at least one resident chunk, so with
`n` classes the retention bound is `n * chunk_min` bytes. At `g = 1.10`
(`77` classes) that bound is 154 MiB of an 8 GB card, at `g = 1.50` it is 46 MiB. Section 5 of cost-model.md works through the trade-off.

## Table E — closed form vs integral over the rounded table

Log-uniform density over `[s_min, s_max]`, 20000 samples, capacity-normalised. `E_int` of Table A is the closed form; this is the
number a log-uniform workload would actually see.

| growth | `k` | closed form | integrated | difference |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.10 | 77 | 4.618% | 4.745% | 0.128 pp |
| 1.25 | 37 | 10.372% | 10.481% | 0.109 pp |
| 1.50 | 23 | 17.790% | 18.028% | 0.239 pp |
| 2.00 | 14 | 27.865% | 27.859% | -0.006 pp |

## Table F — geometric progression vs the shipped union (powers of two)

`E_int` is the integral over the rounded table, log-uniform density,
capacity-normalised (20000 samples); `E_tail` weights each class
equally. Retention is `k · chunk_min`, the §5.2 worst case.

| growth | `k` geometric | `k` union | `E_int` geometric | `E_int` union | delta | `E_tail` union | retention geometric | retention union |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.25 | 37 | 48 | 10.481% | 9.583% | -0.898 pp | 4.066% | 74 MiB | 96 MiB |
| 1.50 | 23 | 34 | 18.028% | 15.009% | -3.019 pp | 2.342% | 46 MiB | 68 MiB |
| 2.00 | 14 | 14 | 27.859% | 27.859% | 0.000 pp | 0.000% | 28 MiB | 28 MiB |

The powers of two never raise the integrated waste, and they lower it wherever the
geometric table does not already contain them, but they add classes: at `g = 1.50`
that is 11 extra classes (22 MiB more worst-case retention, 47.8 % more) for -3.019 pp on a *log-uniform* density — which is
the wrong density to judge them by. They pay on a workload that asks for powers of
two, and `tools/measure_classes.cpp` measures exactly that on the committed trace.
